body.statement: If \(p_{T,H}\) is invariant under the treatment-label flip group, then \(\pi_{iq}(T,H)=1/Q\) for all \(i\in T\) and \(q\in\mathcal Q\), so \(\widehat{\boldsymbol\tau}^{\mathrm{HT}}_T(H)\) equals the ordinary balanced factorial difference-in-means estimator.  With \(H=0\) in both waves, the pooled assignment is exactly uniform on the full-sample balanced support and the pooled estimator is pointwise the full-sample balanced complete-randomization estimator.  No asymptotic limit law is asserted without separate finite-population central-limit and covariance-limit hypotheses.
body.justification: The reduction checks that exact-inclusion analysis preserves the established symmetric factorial design as a special case.
body.gap: The proposition is a required compatibility result rather than a novelty claim; the new content begins when pilot adaptation breaks label symmetry.
body.consumer: Practitioners can use the standard estimator whenever their preregistered score retains the flip symmetry.
body.proof_tex:
Fix a balanced set \(T\), an action \(H\), and a unit \(i\in T\).  Let \(\mathcal G=\{-1,+1\}^{K_f}\) act on treatment labels by coordinatewise multiplication and on assignments by \((g z)_j=g z_j\).  This action preserves \(\Omega_T\), because it merely permutes the \(Q\) treatment cells.  The assumed flip invariance means
\[
p_{T,H}(g z)=p_{T,H}(z),\qquad g\in\mathcal G, z\in\Omega_T.
\]
For \(q\in\mathcal Q\), the definition of the exact inclusion probability and the bijective change of variable \(z=g u\) therefore give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\pi_{i,gq}(T,H)
&=\sum_{z\in\Omega_T}p_{T,H}(z)\mathbf 1\{z_i=gq\}\\
&=\sum_{u\in\Omega_T}p_{T,H}(g u)\mathbf 1\{g u_i=gq\}\\
&=\sum_{u\in\Omega_T}p_{T,H}(u)\mathbf 1\{u_i=q\}
=\pi_{iq}(T,H).
\end{aligned}
\]
The action of \(\mathcal G\) on \(\mathcal Q\) is transitive: for \(q,q'\in\mathcal Q\), choosing \(g=q'\odot q\) gives \(gq=q'\).  Hence \(\pi_{iq}(T,H)\) is constant in \(q\).  Since every assignment assigns unit \(i\) exactly one label, the definition of \(\pi_{iq}\) also yields
\[
\sum_{q\in\mathcal Q}\pi_{iq}(T,H)
=\sum_{z\in\Omega_T}p_{T,H}(z)
  \sum_{q\in\mathcal Q}\mathbf 1\{z_i=q\}
=1.
\]
There are \(Q\) labels, so
\[
\pi_{iq}(T,H)=Q^{-1},\qquad i\in T, q\in\mathcal Q.
\]
In particular, the division in the Horvitz--Thompson formula is valid.  Define the observed treatment-cell mean
\[
\overline Y_T^{\mathrm{obs}}(q)
=\frac{Q}{|T|}\sum_{i\in T:Z_i=q}Y_{in}(q),
\]
which is well defined because balance gives exactly \(|T|/Q\) units in every cell.  Substitution of \(\pi_{iq}=Q^{-1}\) into the definition of \(\widehat{\boldsymbol\tau}^{\mathrm{HT}}_T(H)\) gives, pointwise in the assignment,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{\boldsymbol\tau}^{\mathrm{HT}}_T(H)
&=\frac{1}{|T|}\sum_{i\in T}\sum_{q\in\mathcal Q}
 2^{1-K_f}c_q\,Q\mathbf 1\{Z_i=q\}Y_{in}(q)\\
&=2^{1-K_f}\sum_{q\in\mathcal Q}c_q\,
 \overline Y_T^{\mathrm{obs}}(q).
\end{aligned}
\]
The right-hand side is the ordinary balanced factorial difference-in-means estimator.

It remains to prove the two-wave assertion.  Take the action to be \(H=0\) in each wave.  Then every assignment in \(\Omega_T\) has score
\[
\Delta_T(z)^{\mathsf T}0\,\Delta_T(z)=0.
\]
Thus every assignment lies on the same boundary score.  By the common randomized boundary rule in the definition of \(a_{T,0}\), there is a constant \(c_T\) such that \(a_{T,0}(z)=c_T\) for every \(z\in\Omega_T\).  The exact-acceptance identity in \(\mathrm{def{:}exact\text{-}mixture}\) implies
\[
\alpha=|\Omega_T|^{-1}\sum_{z\in\Omega_T}a_{T,0}(z)=c_T.
\]
Substitution in the positive-support mixture, using \(\alpha>0\), gives
\[
p_{T,0}(z)=|\Omega_T|^{-1}
 \left\{\eta+(1-\eta)\frac{\alpha}{\alpha}\right\}
=|\Omega_T|^{-1}.
\]
Hence both wave assignments are conditionally uniform on their balanced supports; in particular their exact inclusion probabilities are \(Q^{-1}>0\).

Now let \(m\in\mathcal M_n\), put \(N=n-m\), and fix a full-sample balanced assignment \(z\in\Omega_{T_n^{\mathrm{full}}}\).  The definition of \(\mathcal M_n\), together with \(Q\mid n\), ensures that \(m/Q\), \(N/Q\), and \(n/Q\) are integers.  A pilot subset \(S\) is compatible with \(z\) precisely when it contains \(m/Q\) units from each of the \(Q\) treatment cells of \(z\).  Consequently the number of compatible subsets is
\[
L=\prod_{q\in\mathcal Q}{n/Q\choose m/Q}.
\]
For every set of the appropriate size,
\[
|\Omega_S|=\frac{m!}{(m/Q)!^Q},\qquad
|\Omega_{S^c}|=\frac{N!}{(N/Q)!^Q},\qquad
|\Omega_{T_n^{\mathrm{full}}}|=\frac{n!}{(n/Q)!^Q}.
\]
The pilot split is uniform, the pilot assignment is balanced complete randomization, and, conditionally on the pilot history, the zero-action main assignment is uniform by the calculation above.  The chain rule therefore gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr\{Z=z\}
&=\frac{L}{{n\choose m}|\Omega_S||\Omega_{S^c}|}\\
&=\frac{\{(n/Q)!/[(m/Q)!(N/Q)!]\}^Q}
{\{n!/(m!N!)\}\{m!/(m/Q)!^Q\}\{N!/(N/Q)!^Q\}}\\
&=\frac{(n/Q)!^Q}{n!}
=|\Omega_{T_n^{\mathrm{full}}}|^{-1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This probability does not depend on \(z\), so the combined assignment is exactly uniform on the full-sample balanced support.

Finally, for every realized compatible triple \((S,Z_S,Z_{S^c})\), the zero-action inclusion probabilities are \(Q^{-1}\).  The pooled-estimator definition then gives the pointwise identity
\[
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{\boldsymbol\tau}_{n,m}(0)
&=\frac{m}{n}\frac{Q}{m}
  \sum_{i\in S}2^{1-K_f}c_{Z_i}Y_{in}(Z_i)
 +\frac{N}{n}\frac{Q}{N}
  \sum_{i\in S^c}2^{1-K_f}c_{Z_i}Y_{in}(Z_i)\\
&=\frac{Q}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n
 2^{1-K_f}c_{Z_i}Y_{in}(Z_i)
=\widehat{\boldsymbol\tau}^{\mathrm{HT}}_{T_n^{\mathrm{full}}}(0).
\end{aligned}
\]
The last quantity is the ordinary full-sample balanced factorial estimator by the first part.  Its exact-inclusion unbiasedness is also the corresponding special case of \(\mathrm{thm{:}exact\text{-}ht\text{-}accounting}\).  Every argument above is an exact finite-design identity.  No weak-convergence or covariance-limit premise was used, so the conclusion deliberately supplies no asymptotic limit law; such a law requires separate finite-population central-limit and covariance-limit conditions.
